question: What is the browser support status of WebMCP (document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext): which browsers and versions ship it, behind which flags, and where is the spec?
teaser: WebMCP is Chrome-only and still preview: flag chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing; spec is a W3C WebML CG draft; no stable release.

claims.text: The WebMCP spec is a Draft Community Group Report (not a W3C standard) published by the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group at webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp, source repo github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp.
Chrome first shipped WebMCP in Chrome 146 Canary (February 2026) behind a flag; as of October 2026 it remains in Canary with no stable release date announced.
To enable locally in Chrome: set chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing to Enabled and fully relaunch; one third-party source also says an origin trial runs starting Chrome 149.
Chrome for Developers lists WebMCP as available for prototyping to early preview program participants.
Safari and Firefox have not publicly signalled support; Edge is expected to follow Chromium (secondary source).
One blog says the canonical API is document.modelContext as of Chrome 150, deprecating the earlier navigator.modelContext alias (single secondary source).

answer:
WebMCP is a W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group draft (Draft Community Group Report), not a Recommendation. The spec lives at https://webmachinelearning.github.io/webmcp/ with source at https://github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp.

Only Chromium/Chrome has an implementation. It first appeared in Chrome 146 Canary in February 2026 behind a flag, and as of October 2026 it has no announced stable release. For local testing, open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, set it to Enabled and relaunch Chrome fully. The API is only exposed in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost). A third-party guide says an origin trial starts in Chrome 149, and Chrome for Developers offers an early preview program for prototyping.

Safari and Firefox have not publicly committed. Edge, being Chromium-based, is expected to follow Chrome. Naming: the spec defines the surface as a partial interface on Document (document.modelContext); older previews and many articles use navigator.modelContext, and one source says Chrome 150 made document.modelContext canonical and deprecated the navigator alias. Feature-detect both.
